text: Your CI code review system uses Claude to flag potential bugs in pull requests. Developers complain that the 'error handling' category produces so many false positives that they now ignore all findings in that category, including valid ones. The current prompt instructs: 'Be conservative and only report issues you are highly confident about.' What change is most likely to reduce false positives while preserving developer trust?
options: Instruct the model to assign a numeric confidence score to each finding and only display findings above 90% confidence
Add the phrase 'only report high-confidence findings' twice in the prompt to reinforce the conservative instruction

Replace the confidence-based instruction with explicit categorical criteria, such as 'flag missing error handling only when an external call (network, file I/O, database) has no surrounding try/catch or error check'
Increase the extended thinking budget so the model reasons longer before generating each finding
correct_answer: Replace the confidence-based instruction with explicit categorical criteria, such as 'flag missing error handling only when an external call (network, file I/O, database) has no surrounding try/catch or error check'
explanation: Vague conservative instructions like 'be conservative' or 'only report high-confidence findings' do not reliably improve precision because the model's self-assessed confidence is not a good proxy for actual correctness. Explicit, specific categorical criteria that define exactly what qualifies as an issue (and what doesn't) give the model concrete decision boundaries and are far more effective at reducing false positives (option C). Numeric self-reported confidence thresholds (option A) suffer from the same calibration problem as 'be conservative' instructions. Repeating the same vague instruction (option B) doesn't add new information. Extended thinking (option D) may improve reasoning depth but doesn't address the root cause of unclear criteria.

text: You are building an extraction system that classifies customer support tickets into categories and extracts a priority level. Detailed written instructions describing each priority level produce inconsistent classifications across similar tickets. What is the most effective technique to improve output consistency without restructuring the entire pipeline?
options: Add 2-4 few-shot examples showing representative tickets alongside their correct category and priority, including at least one ambiguous case with reasoning for the chosen classification
Increase the `max_tokens` parameter so the model has more room to reason before producing the final classification
Switch to a larger model variant, since classification inconsistency is primarily a function of model capability
Remove the detailed instructions entirely and rely solely on the model's general training to infer appropriate categories
correct_answer: Add 2-4 few-shot examples showing representative tickets alongside their correct category and priority, including at least one ambiguous case with reasoning for the chosen classification
explanation: When detailed prose instructions alone produce inconsistent results, few-shot examples (A) are the most effective technique for achieving consistent, well-calibrated output. Examples that include ambiguous cases with reasoning help the model generalize judgment to novel situations rather than only matching pre-specified patterns. Increasing `max_tokens` (B) doesn't address the root inconsistency issue. Switching models (C) is a costly, unproven fix when a well-known prompting technique hasn't been tried. Removing instructions entirely (D) would likely worsen consistency since the model would lack any grounding for the specific categorization scheme.

text: You are building a document extraction pipeline that processes invoices, receipts, and purchase orders—but the document type is not known in advance for each incoming file. You have defined three separate extraction schemas, one per document type, each implemented as a distinct tool. You need the model to reliably select and invoke exactly one of these extraction tools for every document, never returning plain text instead. Which `tool_choice` configuration should you use?
options: `tool_choice: "auto"`, which allows the model to either call a tool or return a text explanation depending on its assessment of document clarity
`tool_choice` forcing a single named tool, such as `{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"}`, applied uniformly across all incoming documents
Omit `tool_choice` entirely and rely on the system prompt instructing the model to always pick an extraction tool
`tool_choice: "any"`, which forces the model to call one of the available tools but lets it decide which one based on the document content
correct_answer: `tool_choice: "any"`, which forces the model to call one of the available tools but lets it decide which one based on the document content
explanation: `tool_choice: "any"` (option D) guarantees the model will invoke one of the provided tools rather than returning conversational text, while still allowing it to select the appropriate schema based on the document's actual content—exactly what's needed when the document type is unknown ahead of time. `tool_choice: "auto"` (option A) risks the model returning plain text instead of structured output, which breaks the schema-compliance guarantee. Forcing a single named tool (option B) would incorrectly apply the invoice schema to receipts and purchase orders. Omitting `tool_choice` and relying on prompt instructions (option C) is a probabilistic approach that doesn't guarantee tool invocation.

text: Your structured extraction pipeline uses a JSON schema enforced via tool use to pull line items and totals from invoices. Schema validation passes (all required fields are present and correctly typed), but a downstream audit reveals that in 8% of extractions, the sum of extracted line-item amounts does not match the extracted total field. What is the best explanation and remediation approach?
options: This indicates a schema design flaw; switching the total and line-item fields to strings instead of numbers will prevent the mismatch

Tool use with JSON schemas eliminates syntax errors but not semantic errors; add a self-correction step that computes a `calculated_total` from line items and flags discrepancies against the `stated_total` for review or retry
Retry the extraction with the identical prompt and schema, since tool-use-based extraction occasionally produces non-deterministic arithmetic that will self-correct
This is expected behavior and does not require remediation, since schema-validated tool use already guarantees semantic correctness
correct_answer: Tool use with JSON schemas eliminates syntax errors but not semantic errors; add a self-correction step that computes a `calculated_total` from line items and flags discrepancies against the `stated_total` for review or retry
explanation: Strict JSON schemas enforced via tool use guarantee syntactic compliance (correct types, required fields present) but do not prevent semantic errors such as line items that don't sum to the stated total or values placed in the wrong fields. The appropriate remediation is to design the extraction to surface both the stated and calculated values (or a `conflict_detected` boolean) so discrepancies can be flagged for self-correction or human review (B). Changing field types to strings (A) doesn't address the underlying semantic validation gap and would complicate downstream processing. Blind retries without feedback (C) are unlikely to fix a semantic error since the model isn't told what's wrong. Assuming no remediation is needed (D) ignores a known limitation explicitly covered in schema design considerations.

text: Your team runs a nightly extraction job processing roughly 2,000 scanned contracts using the Message Batches API, with results needed by 8 AM for the morning review team (a 10-hour SLA from a 10 PM submission). After the first production run, 6% of documents failed extraction, and investigation shows these were unusually long contracts that exceeded the model's effective context handling for reliable extraction. What is the most appropriate remediation strategy for the failed subset?
options: Identify the failed documents using their `custom_id` values, chunk the oversized contracts into smaller sections, and resubmit only those as a follow-up batch before the SLA deadline
Resubmit the entire original batch of 2,000 documents unchanged, since batch processing occasionally has transient failures that resolve on retry
Switch the entire nightly job to synchronous API calls going forward, since batch processing is unsuitable for any workload with failures
Lower the SLA commitment to 36 hours so there is enough time to manually re-key the failed documents instead of reprocessing them
correct_answer: Identify the failed documents using their `custom_id` values, chunk the oversized contracts into smaller sections, and resubmit only those as a follow-up batch before the SLA deadline
explanation: The `custom_id` field is specifically designed to correlate batch requests and responses, allowing targeted identification of failed documents. Since the root cause is a structural issue (documents too long for reliable extraction), chunking those specific oversized contracts and resubmitting only the failed subset is the efficient fix (A). Resubmitting the entire batch unchanged (B) wastes cost and won't fix a structural failure cause. Abandoning batch processing for the whole workload (C) ignores that batch is well-suited to this latency-tolerant nightly job and overreacts to a fixable, bounded failure rate. Changing the SLA to accommodate manual rework (D) is a costly fallback that avoids addressing the actual fixable root cause.
